steps.prompt: All the parts exist — but it sounds muddy and quiet. What turns it pro?
steps.sub: Two final stages do it: mixing (balance the parts) then mastering (loudness + polish). By the end you'll know what each does, why order matters, and why a permissive model keeps every track copyright-clean.

steps.prompt: Your generated track sounds muddy — the vocal is buried under the bass. First fix?

options.t: Mastering — push the whole track louder and hope the vocal surfaces.
Mixing — balance the levels, EQ and panning so each part has its own space.
Re-record it with a real band.

steps.why: Muddy = a balance problem INSIDE the track, which is exactly what mixing fixes: set levels, carve EQ, and pan parts so the vocal and bass aren't fighting. Mastering can't un-bury a vocal — it works on the finished whole, not the individual parts. Mix first, master second.
hints: The problem is parts fighting each other. Which stage works on the PARTS?
Loudness won't separate two parts that overlap. What balances them?

steps.sub: Tap each card. These three carve space so every part is heard.

cards.b: How loud each part is relative to the others. The vocal should sit on top.
Boost/cut frequencies so parts don't clash — e.g. trim bass so the vocal cuts through.
Place parts left↔right in the stereo field so they don't pile up in the center.

steps.sub: Tap each item, then drop it in the right bin.

items.t: Turn the bass down so it stops drowning the vocal
Bring the whole finished track to -9 LUFS so it's as loud as streaming songs
Pan the rhythm guitar slightly to the left
Apply a limiter to stop the final master from clipping
EQ the kick and bass so they don't clash

hints: If it works on ONE part inside the song, it's mixing.
If it treats the WHOLE finished track as one object (loudness, limiting), it's mastering.

steps.prompt: What's the single most important job of mastering?

options.t: Make it sound consistent and pro-loud on every device — earbuds, phone, car.
Add new instruments the mix was missing.
Translate the lyrics into another language.

steps.why: Mastering polishes the finished mix as one object: bring it to a target loudness and smooth the tone so it holds up everywhere it plays. That cross-device consistency — sounding good on cheap earbuds AND a car system — is the whole point. Adding instruments is a mix/arrangement job, not mastering.
hints: Think about WHERE your track will be heard. What problem does that create?
Mastering is the last polish on the WHOLE track, not a place to add parts.

steps.prompt: Tap the finishing steps in the correct order.
steps.sub: From a rough generated track to a publishable file.
chips: Start from the raw generated multitrack
hints: You must balance the parts BEFORE you polish the whole.
Mastering comes right before the final export.

steps.sub: Tap True or False for each, then check.

statements.t: You should master first, then mix.
statements.why: No — mix first (balance the parts), THEN master (polish the whole). Mastering a badly balanced track just makes the imbalance loud.

statements.t: Mastering helps your track sound consistent across different speakers and devices.
statements.why: Yes — that cross-device consistency is exactly what mastering delivers, so your track holds up on earbuds, phones and car systems alike.

statements.t: Using a permissively-licensed model (e.g. ACE-Step, MIT) makes tracks safe to monetize.
statements.why: Right — a permissive license means the audio it generates is yours to use commercially, so you can publish and earn with low takedown risk. That's 'copyright-clean'.

statements.t: A loud master can rescue a mix where the vocal is completely buried.
statements.why: No — mastering raises the whole track together, so a buried vocal just gets louder while still buried. Fix balance in the MIX first.

hints: Remember the order — which stage comes first?
Why does 'copyright-clean' matter the moment you want to make money from a track?

steps.prompt: Walk a rough track to a publishable file.
steps.sub: Pick the next move at each step. The log fills in as you go.
steps.goal: Finish a generated track so it's pro-loud, clean on every device, and safe to monetize.

turns.situation: You have a raw generated track. The vocal is buried and the kick clashes with the bass.
options: Mix — level, EQ and pan so every part has space
turns.log: 🎚️ Mix → vocal up, EQ kick vs bass, pan guitar

turns.situation: The mix is balanced and clear, but it's noticeably quieter than playlist tracks.
options: Master — bring to target loudness with limiting
turns.log: 📈 Master → -9 LUFS, limiter on, tone smoothed

turns.situation: It's loud and polished. You test it on phone, earbuds and a car.
turns.q: Why does this device check matter?
options: Mastering's job is consistency everywhere — confirm it holds up
turns.log: 🎧 Checks out on phone / earbuds / car

turns.situation: It sounds pro on every device. You're about to publish and monetize it.
options: It was made with a permissively-licensed model — copyright-clean
turns.log: ✅ Permissive license → safe to monetize · export

hints: Order: mix → master → check → export. Don't skip ahead.
The monetization safety comes from the MODEL'S license, not the loudness.

steps.prompt: Tap ALL the jobs that belong to MASTERING (not mixing).
steps.sub: Some of these are mixing jobs. Pick only the mastering ones.
steps.why: Mastering works on the finished whole: target loudness, final limiting, and cross-device consistency. Panning, per-part EQ, and turning down a specific buried part are all MIXING jobs — they act on individual parts inside the track.
hints: Mastering treats the song as ONE object. Mixing touches individual parts.
Anything about a single instrument's level or placement is mixing, not mastering.
